title: Sixty-One Fires
passage:
Ask anyone in the county who dries grain for money which machine burns, and the answer comes back at once: the mixed-flow, the tall one with the ducts inside. This is not folklore. Across nine harvests the fire department’s log records sixty-one dryer fires. Forty-four were in mixed-flow machines, which account for a third of the county’s drying capacity. The explanation is as settled as the count. A mixed-flow dryer walks grain down past staggered rows of inverted-V ducts, and the ducts collect fines – chaff, husk and broken kernel – which sit in hot air and eventually smolder. Clean the ducts weekly, the advice runs, or buy a cross-flow machine and stop worrying.

Ambrose Calverend, an engineer who spent two winters with those sixty-one files for a growers’ cooperative, thinks the count is right and the reason is wrong. The first thing he found was dirt. His team swabbed the duct faces of twenty-six machines that had never burned; per square foot the mixed-flow dryers carried what the cross-flow columns carried, within a few percent. The second was the clock. Burner controllers on thirty-eight machines had kept a data log. In the twenty-nine fires he could time, ignition came after the run was over – a median of forty minutes after the fan stopped. “What I will defend is the timing,” he says. “Why mixed-flow machines dominate the count is a softer argument, and I think it is about who buys them rather than what is inside them.” A mixed-flow costs enough that it goes to operations drying for their neighbors as well as themselves, at so much per ton per point of moisture, and those operations run late and shut down hot.

The firm that builds most of the county’s mixed-flow machines was unmoved. Delphine Grendisham, who runs its service department and has pulled fines out of ducts for eleven years, says the clock is the weak joint in the argument. A controller log ends when the machine stops. The other time in the file is the moment the call came in. On an unmanned site at two in the morning, that is when somebody looked out of a window, not when anything caught. “Set those two numbers side by side and of course the fire looks late,” she says. “It looks late because nobody was there to see it early.” The swabs she reads differently: her crews still take buckets of fines out of ducts in February from machines that swabbed clean in September.

Garrick Tarrowfen, an economist at the growers’ mutual that writes most of the county’s dryer coverage, accepts the swabs and rejects nearly everything else. Cleaning has sold a great many service contracts, he says, and prevented, so far as he can measure, nothing. On that much he and Calverend agree, which puts him across the table from Grendisham, whose buckets he considers beside the point even when they are full. What he will not have is the shutdown. Sort the same sixty-one fires by date rather than by machine, he argues, and the machine stops mattering. Forty-nine fall in a nine-day stretch at the tail of each harvest, when the deduction schedule bites hardest and the elevator’s delivery window is closing. Custom operations work through the tail because that is when the work is there, which is why their machines fill the log. “Calverend has moved the cause from the machine to the shutdown,” Tarrowfen says. “I would move it one step further out, to the contract – and then it stops being an engineering problem.”

The swabs are hard to walk past. The county’s standard advice rests on a difference in dirt that twenty-six machines failed to show, and nobody in the argument now defends it on the old ground. The clock is another matter. Grendisham’s objection has not been answered, and it cannot be answered from files like these; it wants a probe inside a machine that later burns, and nobody has one. Until then Calverend’s account fits the evidence without having been tested by it. What the mutual has to settle before next harvest is narrower. His remedy is nearly free – run the fan on for twenty minutes after the burner cuts – while Tarrowfen’s is not the mutual’s to give, since the deduction schedule belongs to the elevators. Whether writing a run-on clause into next year’s policies would be worth anything turns on something nobody has worked out how to check. What does an operator do at two in the morning on the eighth day of a wet harvest, with trucks waiting and no one there to watch?
– Meredith Ockendale

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: How the price charged for drying grain has moved across nine harvests.
The trouble with investigating fires at sites where nobody is present.
The case for small farms drying their crop rather than hiring it out.
A familiar rule about which dryers burn, and a disputed account of why.

questions.rationale: Whole-text gist. The passage opens by conceding that the trade’s rule of thumb is arithmetically right – forty-four of sixty-one fires in mixed-flow machines that hold a third of capacity – and then spends four paragraphs on a three-way quarrel about the reason: fines in the ducts (Grendisham), the hot shutdown (Calverend), the harvest calendar and the deduction schedule (Tarrowfen). D names both halves, the surviving pattern and the unsettled cause, without picking a winner. A is outside knowledge dressed in passage furniture: charges per ton per moisture point are mentioned once, but no price history is given and none is argued about. B is the scope error – the difficulty of dating a fire on an unmanned site is Grendisham’s single objection in paragraph three, a vivid sub-point promoted to main topic, and it borrows the coda’s ‘no one there to watch’ to feel central. C is a title-plausible theme the text never argues; custom drying appears only as an explanation of who owns mixed-flow machines, never as a practice anyone recommends against.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the duct swabs Calverend’s team took?

options.text: The mixed-flow units held several times as much as the others.
The two kinds of dryer came out about equally dusty inside.
Nothing at all had gathered on the newest ducts.
Too few units were sampled for the comparison to mean much.

questions.rationale: Key B paraphrases the paragraph-two result: per square foot the mixed-flow dryers carried what the cross-flow columns carried, within a few percent. It is a flat, confident claim with no hedge – deliberately, so that ‘pick the cautious option’ misfires here. A is the conventional expectation the swabs defeated, and it tempts because paragraph one has just told the reader that mixed-flow ducts are the dirty ones; a reader running on prior knowledge of dryer fires picks it. C is a quantifier upgrade with an invented target: the finding was parity, not absence, and the passage never sorts machines by age. D is the over-hedged distractor – cautious in form, unsupported in content. Nobody in the passage says the comparison is too small to read: Grendisham’s complaint is that a September swab misses what her crews shovel out in February, which is an argument about when you swab rather than how many machines you swab, and the writer calls the swabs the one thing in the argument that is hard to walk past.

questions.prompt: What does Grendisham say about the times in the fire department’s log?

options.text: They line up closely with what the burner controllers show.
They cover only the machines her crews look after.
They mark when a fire was noticed, not when it began.
They were never intended to be read as evidence at all.

questions.rationale: Key C paraphrases her objection in paragraph three: the second time in every file is the moment the call went in, which on an unmanned site at two in the morning is the moment somebody happened to look out of a window, not the moment anything caught. Her own line – it looks late because there was nobody there to see it early – makes the point again. A reverses her position and recycles the controller vocabulary from paragraph two; the whole force of her argument is that the two clocks do not line up. B fabricates a scope limit out of the fact that she runs a service department, and ‘only’ gives it the shape of a real objection. D is plausible outside knowledge about how incident logs get used – true of many such records, never claimed here, and beside her actual complaint, which is about what the number measures rather than what it was for.

questions.prompt: What is implied about the nine days at the end of each harvest?

options.text: Growers face the same commercial pressure then, whatever they own.
Every fire in the log fell within that stretch.
Dropping the deduction schedule would end the rush and the fires.
Grain arrives faster in those days than the dryers can take it.

questions.rationale: One-inch inference from Tarrowfen’s paragraph. He says the machine stops mattering once the fires are sorted by date, that forty-nine of sixty-one fall in the nine-day tail, that the deduction schedule bites hardest and the delivery window is closing then, and that custom driers keep working through it because that is when the work is. What follows, one step out, is that the squeeze in those days is common to everyone drying, not a property of any particular machine – which is exactly why he wants the cause moved to the contract. B is the quantifier upgrade: forty-nine of sixty-one is a strong majority, not the whole log, and the passage keeps the remaining twelve in view by giving the total twice. C is the two-step leap into policy – Tarrowfen wants the cause relocated, and says the schedule belongs to the elevators, but nobody claims that removing it would stop the fires. D is a plausible-sounding capacity claim the text never makes; the trucks waiting outside belong to the coda’s hypothetical night, not to a stated backlog.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s attitude toward Calverend’s explanation?

options.text: She shares the view that the call records are worthless.
She lays out the three positions and keeps her own counsel.
She counts the old explanation dead and his replacement untested.
She takes the timing result as proved by the county’s files.

questions.rationale: The final paragraph is the writer speaking in her own voice, and it splits Calverend’s case in two. The negative half she accepts: the swabs are hard to walk past, the standard advice rests on a difference in dirt that twenty-six machines failed to show, and nobody now defends it on the old ground. The positive half she withholds: Grendisham’s objection has not been answered and cannot be answered from the files, so his account fits the evidence without having been tested by it. C states both movements. A is the attribution swap – the distrust of the call times is Grendisham’s, and ‘worthless’ overshoots even her; the writer says the files cannot settle the question, not that they are junk. D reverses the verdict and borrows the county’s records to sound grounded. B is the neutral-reporter misread: a writer who declares one explanation dead and calls another untested has taken a position, and she also disposes of Tarrowfen’s remedy as being in nobody’s gift.
